title: Introduction: The Five Key Terms of Dramatism

outline.section: Opening question + the five terms canonically stated
outline.summary: Burke opens with the framing question 'What is involved, when we say what people are doing and why they are doing it?' and immediately names the five terms — Act, Scene, Agent, Agency, Purpose — as the 'generating principle' of the investigation. Each term is glossed by the interrogative it answers: act = what was done; scene = when/where it was done (background, situation); agent = who did it; agency = how he did it / what means or instruments; purpose = why. Burke insists a 'rounded statement about motives' must offer answers to all five questions; men may disagree violently about the values they fill in, but any complete motive-statement is structured by the pentad. The terms are presented as 'understandable almost at a glance' and as resources never to be abandoned, since all motive-assignment can be shown to arise out of them and terminate in them.

outline.section: Wakes-of-launches metaphor + pentad as generating principle
outline.summary: Burke recalls an aerial photograph from the Museum of Modern Art exhibit 'Road to Victory' — two launches proceeding side-by-side on a tranquil sea, their wakes crossing and recrossing in 'an infinity of lines.' Despite the intricacy, the picture conveys simplicity because one perceives the generating principle of its design. The pentad, used as a generating principle, ideally provides a simplicity that can be developed into considerable complexity while remaining discoverable beneath its elaborations. Burke states the work's program: inquire into the purely internal relationships among the five terms — their possibilities of transformation, their range of permutations and combinations — and then observe how these resources figure in actual motive-statements.

Burke distinguishes a Grammar of motives (a concern with the terms alone, with their grammatical resources considered as principles) from philosophies (statements in which the grammatical resources are specifically utilized; treated as casuistries that apply the principles to temporal situations). Scene as a 'blanket term' for any background or setting is 'grammatical'; the choice to name that scene 'God,' 'nature,' 'environment,' 'history,' or 'means of production' is 'philosophical' — a particular philosophic idiom. A statement of grammatical principles may lay claim to universal validity / complete certainty; the choice of any one philosophic idiom embodying the principles is much more open to question. Different cultural situations call for different philosophic idioms as 'temporizing calculus' of motives.

outline.section: Origin of the project (Human Barnyard + trilogy plan)
outline.summary: Burke narrates the project's genesis. The work began as a theory of comedy applied to a treatise on human relations: competitive ambition is over-developed in the modern world; transcendence via appreciation rather than excoriation. Burke took notes on 'the Human Barnyard' — basic stratagems for outwitting or cajoling. The 'you and me' devices were classed as Rhetoric. Notes on modes of expression and appeal in fine arts, plus psychological/psychoanalytic matters, were classed as Symbolic. A residue requiring a grounding 'logically prior to both the rhetorical and the psychological' emerged as the Grammar. The introductory groundwork spun from 'an intended few hundred words into nearly 200,000.' Best illustrations: theological/metaphysical/juridical doctrines (Grammar); forms and methods of art (Symbolic); parliamentary/diplomatic/editorial/sales/social-sparring observations (Rhetoric).

outline.section: Ambiguity-as-resource + great central moltenness alchemy metaphor
outline.summary: Burke names his methodological signature in contrast to the 'terministic ideals of symbolic logic and logical positivism' (terms free of ambiguity). The Grammar takes for granted that human motives are essentially enigmatic and that this enigma manifests in inevitable ambiguities. Therefore the program wants not terms that avoid ambiguity but terms 'that clearly reveal the strategic spots at which ambiguities necessarily arise.' Burke flips the polemical reflex of ambiguity-hunting into a generative principle: distinctions 'arise out of a great central moltenness, where all is merged'; they are 'thrown from a liquid center to the surface, where they have congealed'; an alchemic return to the source remakes molten liquid and enables new combinations. 'A may become non-A' — not by leap but by tracing A back into the ground of its existence (the logical substance that is its causal ancestor) to the point where A is consubstantial with non-A, then re-emerging with non-A. This is the alembic figure: ambiguities are alchemic opportunities.

outline.section: The five terms as attributes of a common ground + transformability
outline.summary: Burke applies the moltenness figure to the pentad: certain formal interrelationships prevail among the five terms by reason of their role as 'attributes of a common ground or substance'; their participation in a common ground makes for transformability. At every point where the field covered by any one term overlaps with another, there is an 'alchemic opportunity' — a doctrine of motivation can be placed in the alembic and another taken out. From the central moltenness emerge such distinctions as freedom/necessity, activity/passiveness, cooperation/competition, cause/effect, mechanism/teleology.

outline.section: Pentad-substitution worked examples (Agent / portrait painter / war / voting)
outline.summary: Burke demonstrates pentad-substitutability via micro-cases. Agent admits subdivision into co-agents (friends) and counter-agents (enemies), and gathers personal properties assigned motivational value (ideas, will, fear, malice, intuition, creative imagination). A portrait painter treats the body as a property of the agent; materialistic medicine treats it as scenic, an objective material; another perspective makes the body an agency by which one gets reports of the world. Machines are obviously agencies, yet in vast accumulation they constitute the industrial scene with its own motivational properties. War can be Agency (means to an end), collective Act (subdivisible into individual acts), Purpose (in war-cults), Scene (situation motivating the inducted soldier's training), or Agent / super-agent (war-god in mythology). Voting is act/agent yet also a politician's medium-or-agency or a part of his scene; if cast without adequate knowledge of consequences it may not be an activity at all but mere passion or motion ('what the behaviorists would call a Response to a Stimulus').

outline.section: Hero-villain-file example + the four casuistic locations
outline.summary: Burke offers the chapter's most fully-worked pentad-substitution: 'The hero (agent) with the help of a friend (co-agent) outwits the villain (counter-agent) by using a file (agency) that enables him to break his bonds (act) in order to escape (purpose) from the room where he has been confined (scene).' In selecting a casuistry, the analyst may locate the motive in (i) the agent (escape credited to love-of-freedom as personality-trait); (ii) the scene (imprisonment-condition awakens thoughts of escape); (iii) the co-agent (motivations reducible to social origins, since the friend's assistance is essential); (iv) the counter-agent (heretical Christians worshipping Judas as saint: betrayal-as-precondition-of-Crucifixion-as-precondition-of-redemption; hero would not have been prodded to escape without villain; 'a bitter fountain may give forth sweet waters'). Each location selects a different philosophic idiom for the same act.

Burke supplies a 'secular variant' of counter-agent motivational reduction: an Engels passage from Anti-Dühring on slavery as the precondition of the division of labor, of Hellenism, of the Roman Empire, of modern Europe ('Without the slavery of antiquity, no modern socialism'). The motivational ancestor in counter-agent location need not be 'outlandish or excessive.' Pragmatists (named: Mead, Dewey) would refer motivation back to agency: the file, the hand holding the file, the brain guiding the hand, the educational system that taught the methods — all are instruments. Mead called his pragmatism a philosophy of the act (note: agency-foregrounding nonetheless titled by Act); Dewey stresses intelligence as instrument (agency, embodied in scientific method), with 'experience' and 'nature' as equivalents of act and scene; Dewey proposes to 'replace the traditional separation of nature and experience with the idea of continuity.'

Burke supplies a second pentad-relational figure: the terms are like fingers, distinct at their extremities but merging in the palm of the hand. To go from any one term to any other without a leap, trace the tendon down into the palm and out along another tendon. Hence no great dialectical enterprise is needed to merge the terms, reducing them to as few as one; then this one is treated as the 'essential' term, the 'causal ancestor,' and the other four are 'deduced' from it across the margins of overlap as its logical descendants. This is the method of metaphysics in the grand style — bringing doctrines to a head in some over-all title (being-in-general, action-in-general, motion-in-general, development-in-general, experience-in-general). There is also an implicit metaphysics that 'often goes by the name of No Metaphysics' and aims at reduction to a presumably underlying atomic constituent. Its vulgar variant is 'unmasking' via 'X is nothing but Y' (where Y is materialistically lower than X).

outline.section: Naming dramatism + synoptic-not-historical + the philosophic-not-empirical claim
outline.summary: Burke names the method 'dramatism' — motives analyzed in a perspective developed from the analysis of drama, treating language and thought primarily as modes of action. The method is synoptic but not in the historical sense (a historical survey would require a universal history of human culture, since every judgment, exhortation, admonition, view, intention, expectation involves assumptions about motive or cause). Synoptic means rather: 'a system of placement' that enables, by systematic manipulation of the terms, the generation or anticipation of the various classes of motivational theory. The treatment reduces the subject synoptically while still permitting appreciation of its scope and complexity. Closing claim: it is not the work's purpose to import dialectical and metaphysical concerns into a subject that might otherwise be free of them — rather to make clear how dialectical and metaphysical issues necessarily figure in motivation. 'The subject of motivation is a philosophic one, not ultimately to be solved in terms of empirical science.'

concepts.label: dramatism
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke's titular method-name: motives analyzed in a perspective developed from the analysis of drama, treating language and thought primarily as modes of action; synoptic-in-the-sense-of-a-system-of-placement rather than historical.

concepts.label: the pentad (five key terms of dramatism)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Act, Scene, Agent, Agency, Purpose — the five irreducible terms naming the constituents of any complete motive-statement; offered as the 'generating principle' of the entire investigation; each answers a single interrogative (what / where-or-when / who / how / why).

concepts.label: Act (pentad term)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: The pentad term naming what took place in thought or deed; answers the question 'what was done?'; designates the action-content of a motive-statement; admits subdivision (collective acts vs. individual acts) and metaphysical foregrounding (Mead's 'philosophy of the act'; Dewey's 'experience'-as-equivalent).

concepts.label: Scene (pentad term)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: The pentad term naming the background or situation in which an act occurred; answers the question 'when or where was it done?'; functions as a blanket name for any setting in which acts or agents are placed; admits philosophic-idiom-substitution (God / nature / environment / history / means of production).
concepts.gloss: where or when it was done

concepts.label: Agent (pentad term)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: The pentad term naming the person or kind of person who performed the act; answers the question 'who did it?'; admits subdivision into co-agents (friends) and counter-agents (enemies); gathers personal properties assigned motivational value (will, fear, malice, intuition, creative imagination).

concepts.label: Agency (pentad term)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: The pentad term naming the means or instruments by which the agent performed the act; answers the question 'how he did it?'; paradigmatic in machines and tools; reducibly extended through pragmatist analysis to hand, brain, educational system as instruments.
concepts.gloss: how he did it / by what means

concepts.label: Purpose (pentad term)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: The pentad term naming the end for the sake of which the act was performed; answers the question 'why?'; subject to violent disagreement among motive-attributors even when the act itself is agreed on; the term over which philosophic-idiom-divergence most readily breaks out.

concepts.label: co-agent
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: An agent (friend / ally) who modifies and so partly motivates another agent's act; Burke's subdivision of Agent in the hero-file example; motivational reduction to co-agents yields a social-origins casuistry.

concepts.label: counter-agent
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: An agent (enemy / villain) whose oppositional action constitutes the precondition of another agent's act; Burke's second subdivision of Agent; motivational reduction to counter-agent yields the heretical-Judas casuistry (betrayal-as-condition-of-redemption) or the Engelsian slavery-as-condition-of-modernity casuistry.

concepts.label: grammar of motives
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: A concern with the pentadic terms alone — their internal relationships, transformations, permutations, and combinations — without reference to the ways their potentialities are utilized in actual motive-statements; the rule-governed terministic substrate that any motive-attribution presupposes.

concepts.label: philosophic idiom
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: A particular philosophic school's specifically utilized casuistry of the grammatical resources: the same grammatical principle of Scene (background) is filled in with 'God' or 'nature' or 'environment' or 'history' or 'means of production' depending on the philosophic idiom; idioms are open to question whereas grammatical principles may lay claim to universal validity.

concepts.label: casuistry (as application of grammatical principles to temporal situations)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke's term for the application of the grammatical resources to a temporal case; any given philosophy is a casuistry of the pentad; a cultural situation extending over centuries is also a 'case' requiring a particular philosophic idiom as its temporizing calculus.

concepts.label: universal-validity-of-grammar vs open-question-of-philosophic-idiom
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke's two-level claim: a statement of the grammatical principles of motivation can lay claim to universal validity (every motive-attribution must reference some background, some actor, some means, some end, etc.), but the choice of any particular philosophic idiom filling in those principles is open to question and varies with cultural situation.

concepts.label: ambiguity as resource (not defect)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke's methodological signature: where logical positivism and symbolic logic seek terms free of ambiguity, the Grammar wants terms that clearly reveal the strategic spots at which ambiguities necessarily arise, because the areas of ambiguity are exactly the areas where transformations among the terms take place.

concepts.label: great central moltenness / alchemic alembic metaphor
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke's master image for terministic transformation: distinctions arise out of a great central moltenness where all is merged, thrown to the surface as congealed crusts; returned to the source they remake into molten liquid and enter new combinations; A becomes non-A by descent to the consubstantial ground and re-emergence.

concepts.label: common ground / common substance of the five terms
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: The five pentad terms participate in a common ground or substance, whose role as their causal ancestor makes them transformable into one another at every point where their fields overlap; this is the formal-metaphysical condition of pentad-substitution.

concepts.label: consubstantiality (proto-)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke's term for the relational condition in which A and non-A share a common substance, becoming traceable into one another via descent to the logical-substance ground; nascent here in the Grammar; will receive full elaboration in the Rhetoric of Motives (1950) as the apparatus of identification.

concepts.label: pentad-overlap / pliancy of the terms / margins of overlap
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: The pliancy among the five terms whereby philosophic systems can 'pull one way and another'; the margins where each term's field overlaps with another are the loci of transformability; figured as the palm-of-hand in the fingers-and-palm metaphor.

concepts.label: fingers-and-palm metaphor
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke's second figure for pentad-relationality: the five terms are like fingers, distinct at the extremities but merging in the palm of the hand; movement from one term to another without leap traces a tendon down into the palm and out along another tendon.

concepts.label: wakes-of-launches metaphor (Road to Victory aerial photograph)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke's opening image for the pentad as generating-principle: an aerial photograph of two launches whose wakes cross and recross 'in almost an infinity of lines,' yet the picture conveys simplicity because the generating principle of the design is immediately perceived; so too the pentad generates considerable complexity from a simplicity discoverable beneath the elaborations.

concepts.label: the pentad as generating principle
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke's structural characterization of the five terms: not five static categories but a generating principle whose internal relationships, transformations, permutations, and combinations produce the full variety of motive-statements; this characterization is the link between the wakes-of-launches metaphor and the casuistic worked examples.

concepts.label: pentad-substitution (categorial recoding of a single referent)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke's operational demonstration that a single referent (war, voting, the body, machines) admits different pentadic codings depending on perspective: war is variously Agency, Act, Purpose, Scene, Agent; the body is Agent-property for the portrait painter, Scene for materialistic medicine, Agency for the sensory-report perspective; voting is Act/Agent yet also Agency/Scene.

concepts.label: casuistic location (selecting which pentad term to locate the motive in)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: The analytic move of selecting in which pentad term to locate the originating motive of an act, given that more than one location is always available; demonstrated in the hero-file example via four candidate locations (agent / scene / co-agent / counter-agent).

concepts.label: the Human Barnyard (origin frame of the project)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke's original working frame: a comedy-of-manners theory applied to human relations; the notebook on the foibles and antics of competitive ambition that grew into the trilogy; the residue of this origin remains in the Grammar's preference for ambiguity-friendly rather than positivist terms.

concepts.label: Grammar / Rhetoric / Symbolic trilogy plan
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke's announced three-volume program: Grammar (theological/metaphysical/juridical illustrations of the formal-prior groundwork); Rhetoric (parliamentary/diplomatic/editorial/sales/social-sparring 'you and me' devices addressed to advantage); Symbolic (modes of expression and appeal in the fine arts, plus psychological/psychoanalytic matters).

concepts.label: metaphysical reduction-to-one (grand-style / titular)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: The method of metaphysics in the grand style: bring doctrines to a head in some over-all title (being-in-general, action-in-general, motion-in-general, development-in-general, experience-in-general), distributing the other terms about this titular term in positions leading up to it and away from it.

concepts.label: implicit-No-Metaphysics (reduction to atomic constituent)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke's diagnosis of the implicit metaphysics that goes by the name of No Metaphysics: reduction not to an over-all title but to a presumably underlying atomic constituent; vulgar variant is the 'X is nothing but Y' technique of unmasking (Y materialistically lower than X).

concepts.label: synoptic-as-system-of-placement
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke's specification of the work's synopticity: not a historical universal-survey (which the subject would require if approached historically) but a system of placement enabling, via systematic manipulation of the terms, the generation or anticipation of the various classes of motivational theory.

concepts.label: motivation is philosophic, not empirical-scientific
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke's closing programmatic claim: dialectical and metaphysical issues necessarily figure in motivation; the subject is not ultimately to be solved in terms of empirical science; the Grammar's argument occupies a properly philosophic register.

concepts.label: language and thought as modes of action (dramatism's core ontological commitment)
concepts.definition_paraphrastic: Burke's foundational gloss for why dramatism is the right titular word for the method: language and thought are treated primarily as modes of action rather than as modes of representation; this is what licenses the analysis of motive-statements via the terms of drama.

positions.claim: Motives are grammatical-terministic, not psychological-empirical: any complete statement about motive must answer all five pentadic questions (what / where-or-when / who / how / why), and what differs across cases is not the questions but the values assigned and the foregrounded term.
positions.critique_target: implicit critique of empirical-psychological motive-theories and behaviorist stimulus-response reductions (the behaviorists named at p.xx)

positions.claim: Grammatical principles of motivation may claim universal validity (every motive-statement must reference some background, etc.); particular philosophic idioms filling in those principles (God / nature / environment / history / means of production for Scene) are open to question and vary with cultural situation.
positions.critique_target: implicit critique of any one philosophic idiom claiming uniquely-correct ontology of motive; also critique of symbolic logic and logical positivism's universalist terminological ambitions

positions.claim: Where logical positivism / symbolic logic seek to abolish terminological ambiguity, the Grammar wants terms that clearly reveal where ambiguity necessarily arises, because ambiguity is the precondition of transformation among the terms; ambiguities are alchemic opportunities, not defects.
positions.critique_target: symbolic logic and logical positivism (named at p.xviii); also the polemical idol-smashing of one-philosophic-term-as-too-ambiguous when the smasher's own preferred term is equally ambiguous

positions.claim: The five terms are mutually transformable because they participate in a common ground or substance; their pliancy across the margins of overlap is the analytic engine of dramatism; metaphysical systems exploit this pliancy by reducing the five to one and deducing the others from it as causal descendants.
positions.critique_target: grand-style metaphysical reduction-to-one (being / action / motion / development / experience as titular over-all terms); also the implicit No-Metaphysics reduction to atomic constituent ('X is nothing but Y' unmasking)

positions.claim: The Grammar is synoptic in the sense of a system of placement (enabling generation or anticipation of the classes of motivational theory by systematic manipulation of the terms), not in the sense of a historical universal-survey; the synoptic reduction permits appreciation of scope and complexity rather than collapsing them.
positions.critique_target: any historical-or-empirical-survey method of motive-theory cataloguing; implicit critique of social-scientific motivational empiricism

positions.claim: Motivation is a philosophic subject, not ultimately to be solved in terms of empirical science; dialectical and metaphysical issues necessarily figure in motivation; the Grammar's argument therefore properly occupies the philosophic register.
positions.critique_target: behaviorism (named at p.xx as treating voting as Response-to-Stimulus); empirical motivational science generally

philosophers_cited.name: G. H. Mead
philosophers_cited.burke_move: Named as pragmatist whose 'philosophy of the act' demonstrates that agency-foregrounding analysis can nonetheless be titled by Act — illustrates the metaphysical reduction-to-one method where one term is causal-ancestor and the others descend. Tier-B in Phase 0; here a confirming citation.

philosophers_cited.name: John Dewey
philosophers_cited.burke_move: Named with quote-paraphrase 'replace the traditional separation of nature and experience with the idea of continuity' (Intelligence and the Modern World cited). Dewey foregrounds intelligence as instrument (agency); 'experience' and 'nature' are his act/scene equivalents. Burke uses Dewey to illustrate scene-act overlap-stressing within a pragmatist agency-featuring framework.

philosophers_cited.name: Friedrich Engels
philosophers_cited.burke_move: Block-quoted directly from Anti-Dühring on slavery as precondition of division-of-labor, Hellenism, Roman Empire, modern Europe ('Without the slavery of antiquity, no modern socialism'). Burke uses Engels as the 'secular variant' of counter-agent motivational reduction (parallel to the heretical-Christian Judas case).

philosophers_cited.name: the behaviorists (Watson/Skinner lineage, unnamed)
philosophers_cited.burke_move: Named generically: 'what the behaviorists would call a Response to a Stimulus.' Burke uses the behaviorists as a foil — voting cast without adequate knowledge may not be activity at all but mere passion or motion; Burke implies critique of the stimulus-response reduction by demoting it to 'sheer motion,' positioning behaviorist analysis as the under-act limit-case.

philosophers_cited.name: Christian heretics who worshipped Judas as saint
philosophers_cited.burke_move: Cited as example of counter-agent casuistic location: Judas's betrayal-as-precondition-of-Crucifixion-as-precondition-of-redemption. Burke uses the heretical case to demonstrate that counter-agent motivational reduction is a real (not outlandish) analytic option.

philosophers_cited.name: symbolic logic / logical positivism
philosophers_cited.burke_move: Named generically as the foil for Burke's ambiguity-friendly project: the 'terministic ideals' of symbolic logic and logical positivism seek terms free of ambiguity; the Grammar by contrast wants terms that reveal where ambiguities necessarily arise.

literary_examples.burke_move: The opening figure for the pentad as generating-principle: intricacy of crossing wakes resolves into simplicity once the generating principle of the design is perceived.

literary_examples.name: The hero-villain-co-agent-file fable (Burke's invented example)
literary_examples.burke_move: The Intro's most fully-worked pentad-substitution illustration: 'The hero (agent) with the help of a friend (co-agent) outwits the villain (counter-agent) by using a file (agency) that enables him to break his bonds (act) in order to escape (purpose) from the room where he has been confined (scene).' Four candidate casuistic locations demonstrated (agent / scene / co-agent / counter-agent).

tensions.summary: The Grammar's signature two-level claim: at the grammatical level the principles claim universal validity (every motive-statement must have a Scene); at the philosophic-idiom level the choice of which philosophic idiom fills in the principle (God / nature / means of production for Scene) is open to question. Tension: how can the grammatical level be 'universally valid' if every actually-occurring motive-statement is always already cast in a particular idiom — and the idiom is exactly what supplies the determinate Scene? Burke's resolution is that the grammatical principles are necessary conditions of intelligibility, not contentful claims; the idioms are the contentful claims, and they are what arguments are over.

Burke wants the pentad's pliancy / common-substance grounding (which makes A become non-A via descent to logical-substance ground) to be a feature, not a vice — alchemic opportunity. But the same pliancy is exactly what licenses the grand-style metaphysics' reduction-to-one (being / action / motion / experience as over-all titles) and the implicit-No-Metaphysics's reduction-to-atomic-constituent ('X is nothing but Y'), both of which Burke positions as problematic. Tension: how does Burke's own dramatistic synoptic reduction differ from these other reductions, given that they share the underlying mechanism of cross-margin transformation? Burke's answer is that dramatism makes the pliancy explicit and refuses to causally privilege any one term as ancestor.

Burke at p.xx demotes inadequately-informed voting to 'sheer motion (what the behaviorists would call a Response to a Stimulus),' implying a hierarchy in which act presupposes a threshold of knowledge / intention. But the pentad framework's grammatical-universality claim requires that any motive-statement be analyzable in terms of all five terms — and a Response to a Stimulus is, on Burke's own setup, still an act (it has an agent, a scene, an agency, a purpose, however reduced). Tension: is the act/motion distinction grammatical (a feature of which level of motive-statement is in play) or substantive (a real metaphysical threshold)? This tension recurs through Part 2.III and Part 3.II.

Burke names dramatism a 'titular word' for the method, with motives analyzed 'in a perspective that, being developed from the analysis of drama, treats language and thought primarily as modes of action.' Tension: is this a metaphor (motive-analysis as if it were drama-analysis) or an ontological claim (language and thought are in fact modes of action, hence drama-analysis is the appropriate method)? The closing 'motivation is a philosophic subject, not empirical' suggests the latter, but Burke's resistance to grand-style metaphysics (which would require a positive ontological claim) suggests caution about reading dramatism as ontology.
